findings.title: Cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs without justification
findings.body: This changes the interval for CleanUpService.Run from 10 minutes to 1 minute. That ticker drives every job in clean(), not only annotation cleanup: expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, temp-user invites, short URLs, and query-history enforcement will now run 10x as often, increasing database and log load in every Grafana instance. The PR description only justifies splitting the annotation DELETE statements to avoid MySQL deadlocks and does not mention or justify this frequency change, so it looks like a leftover local-testing change and should be reverted or separately justified and scoped to annotations.

findings.title: Normal cleanup batches are logged at Error level with the full ID list
findings.body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags unconditionally call r.log.Error before and after every batch (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including successful batches and the final empty batch where err is nil and affected is 0. Normal periodic cleanup will therefore flood error logs, trigger error-based alerting/log pipelines, and serialize ID slices that can contain up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (tested at 32767) entries per batch. These diagnostic messages should be Debug level, should not log the full ID slice, and errors should only be logged/returned when the batch actually fails.

findings.title: Parameter-limit workaround only handles SQLite, regressing large batches on other databases
findings.body: deleteByIDs binds one '?' placeholder per fetched ID for every database except the special-cased SQLite path at lines 608-613. The previous implementation used a subquery DELETE with no per-ID bind parameters. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configurable and this PR's own test raises it to 32767; a larger configured batch (over 65535 parameters) will now fail on PostgreSQL/MySQL with bind-parameter limits even though the old statement would have succeeded, aborting cleanup partway. The workaround should be based on len(ids) and the actual database's parameter limit, or IDs should be chunked/inlined for all affected dialects.

findings.title: SQLite inline ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation
findings.body: For SQLite with batch size over 999, deleteByIDs builds the IN list by repeatedly doing values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) in a loop. Each iteration copies the entire accumulated string, so building a list of up to batch-size IDs (32767 in the added test, applied repeatedly to annotations and orphaned tags) is O(n^2) in time and allocations and can make large cleanups and the new test very slow. Use strings.Builder (or chunk the deletes) instead of re-formatting the whole string per ID.
